# Nuthatch - full description

Nuthatch is a self-hosted-first, AI-native blockchain indexer. One Rust binary, one command,
a live indexed API. There is no mandatory third-party data dependency, ever. Tagline: "Be your
own indexer." Status: **v4.0.2**, the stable line - a promise about stability (from 4.0.0 to the last
4.x release a config keeps working with the same meaning, a data directory upgrades in place with no
re-index or migration command, and no HTTP route, response field, generated table or column, or MCP
tool is removed, renamed or retyped; upgrade only, and the off-by-default cargo features and the SQL
dialect's functions, which are DuckDB's, are not covered), not a claim of completeness. Licence: MIT OR Apache-2.0.

This document is written for language models and agents. It separates what the binary does
today from the design targets. Do not present a design target as a present-tense capability,
and do not infer benchmark numbers, star counts, or testimonials from it.

## The problem it addresses

Applications that read a blockchain need an index: a layer that turns blocks and transactions
into balances, positions, holders, and history. Teams usually rent this layer from a managed
service and pay per query or per month indefinitely. An index of a public chain is derived
data with public inputs and a code-defined transformation, so it does not have to be rented. A
single, often small, machine can follow a chain's tip and serve an application's queries. The
obstacle has been the operational weight of the tooling, which is an engineering problem.

## What it is

- A single static Rust binary. Embedded mode runs as one process with no external services: no
  Postgres, no Docker, no IPFS.
- It works against any RPC endpoint today (public defaults, round-robin failover). A reth ExEx
  mode against your own colocated node is designed and stubbed, not yet wired.
- No gateway, no metered data API, no API tokens, no telemetry.
- Free and licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 (at your option). There is no hosted tier, no token, and no pricing page.

## What it does today

1. `nuthatch init 0xAddr [0xAddr…] --chain <mainnet|arbitrum-one|base|bsc|polygon|gnosis|optimism|monad|robinhood>`
   - resolves each contract's
   ABI (Sourcify first, then an Etherscan-class API, cached; EIP-1967/legacy-OZ proxies resolved)
   and scaffolds a multi-contract nest: `nuthatch.toml`, `abis/`, a `schema.json`, a `semantic.toml`
   (per-nest meaning, seeded from the ABI), a commented `views/` starter, an `llms.txt`, and a Claude
   Code skill. Omit `--chain` and it probes each supported chain for the contract's bytecode. It does
   not yet auto-generate the view logic, handlers, or tests from the ABI.
2. `nuthatch dev` - polls logs over RPC (round-robin failover, adaptive `getLogs` chunking), decodes
   every declared event of every contract (topic0 registry → one table per `{alias}__{event}`, an
   empty typed table even before a declared event has fired),
   stores rows in an embedded hot store (redb), seals finalized ranges to content-addressed Parquet
   (pruning the hot store), and serves a local HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:8288: `/tables`,
   `/table/{name}` (hot+cold merged), `/schema` (the enriched data model), `/sql` (read-only DuckDB,
   sealed history UNION the live hot tip), `/explain` (validate SQL without running it), `/entity/{id}`,
   `/balances`, `/balance/{addr}`, `/exposure/{addr}`, `/flags`, `/ready` (readiness: 200 fresh / 503
   stalled), `/metrics` (Prometheus), and a localhost-gated admin UI at `/_admin/`. Every row carries provenance columns (`block_hash`,
   `_seq`, `block_timestamp`) and `*_dec`/`*_overflow` siblings. The balance view is DBSP-maintained
   in i128 (decimal-string serialised); a reorg is a retraction; the view replays from stored facts
   on restart. `dev --seal-direct` writes finalized history straight to Parquet, resolves declared
   `[[calls]]`, and produces the same sealed bytes as the hot-store path. The former ~8.7x
   seal-direct and ~20x stacked multipliers were withdrawn in 2.7.0 after their denominator was
   traced to an obsolete harness path.
3. Nests: `nuthatch init --from <git-url | ./dir>` runs a published nest (vendored ABIs + deployment
   blocks, schema-version guarded); authored `views/*.sql` (RFC-0018) are a validated, drift-gated
   layer (each binds against the schema at load, so a moved column is a loud `nuthatch check` failure,
   described in `semantic.toml`, surfaced in `/schema`); `nuthatch check` also runs `checks/*.sql`
   against recorded fixtures. `nuthatch nest bundle`/`load` build and verify a content-addressed,
   portable nest `.bundle` (loadable from a file or a URL). **There is no `roost` subcommand - it was
   removed in 2.0, not renamed.** One `nuthatch dev --dir <dir>` runs one nest or many depending on
   whether the directory holds a `nuthatch.toml` or a `mounts.toml`, with per-nest isolation and a
   per-cursor RSS budget (RFC-0012 + RFC-0032, verified live on Arbitrum). Nest data is keyed by
   content address at `data/<nid>/` and a mount by `(tenant, nid)`, so two mounts share one dataset
   and it is never indexed twice; unmounting one of two decrements a reference, and `nuthatch prune`
   reclaims what nothing mounts. `nuthatch migrate` moves a pre-2.0 directory across. A tenant is an
   opaque ownership label - no identity, no authentication, no quotas, no metering.
   A nest may also declare an authored incremental entity in `entities.toml` (RFC-0041, stable in
   3.0.0): one admitted `SELECT`, a unique output key and `max_rows`, maintained as blocks arrive
   and retracted on reorg. It is queryable by name from `/sql` and via `/derived/{entity}`, and has
   per-entity applied-through/current/rows/faulted/unavailable/progress metrics. It is not an
   authored view: views run at query time. Entity state seeds from local sealed history on restart;
   `dev --seal-direct` refuses a nest declaring an entity.
4. `nuthatch transform <component.wasm>` - runs a pure, zero-capability WASM transform over an Arrow
   batch; effectful stages take per-component capability grants (`kv` today). `nuthatch mcp` -
   serves the Model Context Protocol over stdio (12 tools: status, schema, tables, table, sql,
   explain, entity, balance, top_balances, flags, exposure, screen_status; plus 3 resources -
   nuthatch://schema|tables|status - and 3 prompts: profile-contract, investigate-address,
   verify-a-number). Governed semantic layer (RFC-0016): the `schema` tool serves this nest's
   meaning; failed queries return fix hints and `explain` validates without executing; results carry
   a citable provenance stamp.
5. Factories and dynamic contract discovery (RFC-0009): `[[templates]]`/`[[factories]]` index the
   child contracts a factory deploys at runtime - tip, backfill, reorg-safe, with a
   `{template}__children` view. It indexes Uniswap.
6. Compliance pack (RFC-0008): sanctions screening against content-addressed list snapshots
   (`nuthatch screen`, replayable `sanction_hit` annotations), threshold/velocity flags at `/flags`,
   counterparty exposure at `/exposure/{addr}`, alert webhooks over a durable at-least-once outbox,
   and a signed pack manifest (`pack build`/`verify`, ed25519) with `audit replay`/`report`.
7. Admin UI and webhooks (RFC-0010): an embedded read-only admin UI at `/_admin/` (no framework/CDN,
   localhost-gated), plus user `[[webhooks]]` POSTing sealed rows matching a `where` clause,
   HMAC-signed via `X-Nuthatch-Signature`.
8. The nest registry (RFC-0019): publish and pull nests by `name@version` from a filesystem or S3
   backend, content-addressed end to end.
9. Safe upgrades, no resync tax (RFC-0020): `nest diff` classifies an update compatible or breaking;
   `nest upgrade` hot-swaps a compatible one with an atomic endpoint flip once the new version
   catches up - reusing the old sealed segments when decode is unchanged, so it costs seconds rather
   than days - and serves a breaking one at a new endpoint while the old carries RFC-8594
   `Deprecation`/`Link` headers.
10. Multichain runtimes (RFC-0021): `[[chains]]` in `mounts.toml` hosts nests across more
    than one chain in one runtime, with one isolated cursor per chain (own tip, finality, reorg
    boundary) and a per-cursor footprint budget. It is a capability, not a mandate - one chain per
    runtime is the default, and a cursor is never multiplexed across two chains.
    Since 3.13.0 the runtime owns the nest lifecycle: it may start with nothing mounted, and a caller
    hands it a NID over the admin API (`POST /_admin/nests`), which it fetches from `--registry`,
    verifies, installs, catches up and serves, as a job readable at `GET /_admin/mounts/<name>`.
    Mounts can be priced first (`?dry_run=true`), suspended and resumed, moved to a new NID with no
    gap (`/_admin/move`), and unmounted with their disk reclaimed. Guide: /docs/operate/hosting-nests/.
11. Derive-first contract reads (RFC-0023, tiers 1-3): `nuthatch recipe add total_supply|balances|
    holder_count|reserves` derives from indexed events what a subgraph pays an archive node to
    `eth_call` for - no archive node, no eth_call. `nuthatch metadata fetch` calls once and caches
    the immutable reads (`decimals`/`symbol`/`name`). Tier 3 shipped in 2.6.0: a `[[calls]]` block
    reads contract state via `eth_call` **pinned to a fixed block**, so a value that genuinely cannot
    be derived is still reproducible rather than whatever the chain says today. A `[[calls]]` block
    is either sampled (one fixed calldata every N blocks) or row-driven (RFC-0038 §3: one call per
    row of a table at that row's block, arguments from the row's columns - what a mapping's
    `balanceOf(event.params.to)` does). Since 2.7.0 all
    streaming and seal-direct paths resolve it, and both benchmark arms require `--state-rpc` rather
    than silently skipping the work. Tier 4 (a local
    execution engine, RFC-0024) is designed and deferred.
12. Adaptive MCP tool advertisement (RFC-0025): `GET /shape` reports what a nest can actually answer
    and the MCP bridge filters `tools/list`/`prompts/list` to match, so an agent is never handed an
    inert tool. Fails open if the probe fails.
13. Fault quarantine and partial health (RFC-0026): a faulting nest is quarantined, not fatal -
    healthy siblings keep indexing and serving, and a retryable fault is re-admitted on a backoff. A
    nest's error no longer kills its cursor and a cursor's death no longer kills the runtime. Surfaced
    at `GET /nests` (live per-nest health merged per request), runtime-root and per-nest `/ready`, and
    the `nuthatch_nest_health` / `nuthatch_nest_quarantine_total` / `nuthatch_cursor_live` metrics.
    `--fail-fast` restores exit-on-first-fault for CI and deterministic tests.
14. Publishing sealed segments (RFC-0052, 3.7.0): `nuthatch publish sync --target <dir |
    s3://bucket/prefix>` mirrors every segment that is not provisional to `<target>/<data identity>/`,
    writing Parquet first, then the catalogue byte for byte, then `publish.json`. `publish verify`
    checks every published object against the local catalogue (`--deep` downloads and re-hashes each
    one; `--etag-md5` compares ETags on a store whose ETag is the object's MD5, such as AWS S3 without
    SSE-KMS or SSE-C, or MinIO), and `publish status` prints local and remote `sealed_through` and what
    is still to upload, writing nothing. `dev` and `serve` publish continuously with
    `--publish-target`, `--publish-interval` and `--publish-parallelism`; a runtime directory takes the
    same settings per mount from `[mounts.publish]` in `mounts.toml`. The mirror runs on its own
    thread, so a slow bucket delays the mirror and never a seal. Credentials are the usual `AWS_*`
    variables. A published prefix is plain Parquet plus a catalogue; CI publishes to a real MinIO and
    requires Trino's counts and sums over the prefix to match DuckDB's.
15. `nuthatch emit dune --dir <nest> --out <dir> --source <namespace>` (RFC-0055, 3.7.0): one plain
    DuneSQL `SELECT` per event table over `dune.<namespace>.<table>`, written offline and
    deterministically. Each column is cast to its DuneSQL type, every wide integer keeps its exact
    text beside it as `<name>_raw`, and implicit columns take Dune's `evt_*` names. Views, call tables
    and block tables are not emitted. The queries push interpretation, not rows: they do not by
    themselves put data in Dune. Since 3.8.3 an authored view in `views/*.sql` is emitted too when its
    translation is exact: DuckDB's parser reads the view and the query is rendered again from an
    allowlist of constructs that return the same result in DuckDB and Trino. Every other view is
    listed under "Not emitted" in the output `README.md` with the construct that stopped it.
16. IPFS documents at scale (RFC-0037 slices 5 to 8, 3.8.0): `[[ipfs]]` takes `cid_json_path` (the
    key holding the CID) and `json_match` (resolve only objects whose string fields equal the given
    values), and the source can be an event column or a top-level call's calldata. Every document
    resolves out of band behind the cursor, with retry, backoff and a recorded give-up after 10
    failures, and sealing holds below any block whose documents are neither stored nor given up on.
    A multi-block document is proven by re-encoding it in Kubo's default layout or by hashing each
    block of a CAR against its CID; an unproven document writes no row and is retried. `[ipfs.rows]`
    explodes a proven JSON document into one typed row per element, in a table of its own, and
    `keep_content = false` drops the raw JSON. Since 3.8.2, every retried fetch is logged and counted
    (`nuthatch_nest_ipfs_retries_total`), a `--seal-direct` window waits at most
    `--ipfs-window-deadline` (300 s, `0` for none) for one document, and `GET /ipfs/gave-up?limit=`
    lists documents given up on. A document given up on is absent from sealed history and is not
    fetched again.
17. Store coverage check (3.8.4): beside the registry hash, a nest records its chain and chain id,
    each contract's address and start block, its factories and its extraction settings in the store
    as `indexed_coverage`, and refuses to start a store holding data when `nuthatch.toml` no longer
    matches, naming each part that moved. The first start after upgrading records rather than
    verifies. RPC endpoints and the nest's name are not checked. `/` and `/nest` show `nid` and
    `data_identity`.
18. `nuthatch nest nid` (3.9.0) prints the identity a nest's data is stored under (`data/<nid>/`)
    without running it. `nuthatch offchain pull <url> --table <name> --format json` (3.9.0, RFC-0045
    stage 2) fetches a JSON-array feed once and seals it as an offchain snapshot, for a host timer to
    run; an authored entity can read `offchain__<table>` as a source, and a snapshot is read only
    after its bytes match the manifest hash.
19. RPC economy (3.11.0): a backfill takes `block_timestamp` from the logs where the endpoint supplies
    it rather than buying a header per block; idle polls skip the reorg check; the default poll
    interval is the chain's block time (never below 2 s; `--poll-interval` overrides it, and `/ready`
    reports the source); `--rpc-fallback` names endpoints asked only while every other endpoint is
    failing.

Chains: Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One (42161), Base (8453), BSC (56), Polygon (137), Gnosis (100),
Optimism (10), Monad (143) and Robinhood Chain (4663) are built in - keyless public
endpoints, a tuned `eth_getLogs` window, per-chain finality policy, and bytecode probing so `init`
can detect which of them a contract lives on (it probes all nine when you omit `--chain`). Any
other EVM chain also works: `nuthatch init 0xAddr --chain <name> --rpc <url>` reads the chain id
from the endpoint itself. An unlisted chain inherits depth-64 finality and a 20-block
`getLogs` window (raise it with `--window`), and its `chain_id` is verified against every endpoint at
startup - a mixed-chain pool is refused, since indexing against the wrong chain corrupts state
silently. The bundled free public RPCs exist so `init` → `dev` works with zero setup; they are
rate-limited, shared, sometimes fail by returning an empty result rather than an error, and are
unsuitable for deep backfills or production - use your own node or a paid provider for real work.
Measured footprint (not a target): ~37 MB single contract, ~58 MB three-contract 23-table nest -
2.8% of the ≤2 GB per-cursor CI budget (the `footprint` job fails above 256 MB). Backfill paths are
correctness-gated to produce byte-identical sealed segments; no storage-path multiplier is currently
claimed because a harness correction invalidated the old baseline and public-RPC remeasurement
disagreed. On Sentio's **OBIB** benchmark, case 1 (LBTC `Transfer`, 22.2M Ethereum
blocks) completes in **74.8 s** for **294,278 events** in **321 RPC requests** at 320 MB peak RSS
against a real provider - the event count matching Sentio's own README. v4.0.2 is the current release,
with prebuilt binaries for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Linux x86_64 and container images at
`ghcr.io/nightswatchhq/nuthatch`. Minimum supported Rust version is 1.95.

**Two security patches matter when advising on a version**, both on `/sql` (which binds 127.0.0.1 by
default): **v0.9.3** fixes an **arbitrary file read** - DuckDB accepts a quoted function name and the
guard matched only an unquoted one, so `SELECT * FROM "read_csv"('/etc/passwd')` executed, and every
earlier release is affected - and **v0.6.2** fixes an **arbitrary file write** via `;`-stacked
`COPY … TO`. Apart from the 3.7.0, 3.8.0, 3.9.0 and 3.10.0 exceptions (under Install), upgrading the binary is a plain swap: on-disk state is forward-readable and the `dev`
flags are stable, so there is no migration or re-backfill.

## Not built yet (design targets)

reth ExEx tip-ingestion (own node; toolchain + dependency blockers cleared, needs a synced node)
and firehose-class extraction of traces and state diffs on top of it (RFC-0014, deferred);
**replacing DuckDB with Burrmill**, a Rust query engine built on DataFusion (decided 2026-09-26,
reversing the August "Keeping DuckDB" post; RFC-0013's gate had found DataFusion alone 1.6-2.7x
DuckDB's latency). An engine trait and a shadow session, in which Burrmill answers beside DuckDB and
DuckDB's answer is served, are on main behind a feature off in release builds; cutover waits on a
release cycle of real traffic with zero unexplained differences. Every release to date, including
v4.0.2, answers SQL with DuckDB, so do not describe a released nuthatch as running on DataFusion or
Burrmill;
streaming subscribe (SSE); local AI models (Ollama / bring-your-own-key); effectful HTTP egress for
transform worlds (`kv` grant ships today); wildcard indexing.

GraphQL (RFC-0053) is no longer a design target: 3.7.0 shipped a partial read surface, exact for a
subgraph's event-shaped fields and a named refusal for the rest, and it is parked. Since 3.10.0 the
GraphQL routes exist only in a build with `--features graph`; the published binary and images answer
them with 404. An analytics client cannot adopt it unmodified, because GraphQL refuses a whole query for one unanswerable field.
Do not describe it as a drop-in replacement.

## Architecture

The ingestion source sits behind a trait, so an ExEx source is a new impl rather than a fork of
the indexing logic. A storage trait for scaled mode is planned in the same shape.

- Embedded mode (default, built): one process. Ingestion (RPC extraction today; a reth ExEx
  when colocated, designed) -> deterministic decode -> a hot store (redb) for entity point-reads
  near the tip -> content-addressed Parquet segments sealed strictly past finality -> an embedded
  DuckDB that attaches those segments read-only for analytical SQL. DuckDB is single-writer: only
  the ingestion thread writes; queries attach read-only.
- Scaled mode (built, RFC-0022): the same crates with Postgres in place of redb for the hot store,
  run as three roles - a control plane holding desired state, a writer pool taking **one lease per
  chain cursor** with the fence enforced inside the store's own write transaction, and an
  independently-scaled query tier. Workers **pull the nests they are assigned** from a registry; a
  pinned `bundle_hash` is fetched by content address, so re-tagging a version cannot change what the
  fleet runs. Verified across real machines, including 377 blocks indexed through a 90-second
  control-plane outage. The query engine is DuckDB in both modes in every release to date; its
  replacement by Burrmill is described under design targets.

Reorg strategy: reorgs only ever touch the mutable hot store, and become retractions in the
incremental view. Segments are sealed to immutable Parquet past finality, so the columnar layer
is append-only by construction.

## Determinism and verifiability

Decoding, reorg handling, and entity derivation are deterministic and re-executable: identical
block inputs always produce identical stored state. Entity authoring:

- Declarative (built, default for balances): entities are incremental views over decoded events,
  maintained incrementally. Reorgs are retractions; backfills are the same circuit run as a batch.
- Imperative (built, escape hatch): capability-isolated WASM components via WIT (language-agnostic
  by design), operating on batches (Arrow) and emitting batches of facts. Components are pure
  functions with all state held host-side.

Capability isolation makes purity checkable from a component's imports alone: a component granted
zero capabilities is pure and may feed entity derivation; effectful components (for example HTTP
enrichers) produce annotations only, never canonical entities - that effectful path is designed,
not built. Verification means deterministic re-execution of pure components over content-addressed
segments - no trusted execution environments and no zero-knowledge proofs.

## AI-native, without phone-home

- A built-in MCP server is compiled into the binary: schema discovery, table listing and reads, SQL
  execution, entity and balance lookup, plus compliance flags, counterparty exposure, and sanctions
  screening (12 tools, 3 resources, 3 prompts). It works fully offline, bridging to a running local instance.
- `init` ships an `llms.txt` and a Claude Code skill so coding agents get the real query surface
  instead of guessing. Generating an indexer with tests from an ABI is a design target.
- Local models via Ollama or a bring-your-own key are planned. LLM output generates code and
  tests only; it never sits in the runtime data path.

## Comparison, stated as facts

| | Needs a subgraph | Needs handler code | Data comes from | What you run | Query with |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The Graph** | yes | yes (AssemblyScript) | indexers on the network | nothing, or graph-node + Postgres + IPFS | GraphQL |
| **Ponder** | no | yes (TypeScript) | your RPC endpoint | Node.js, plus Postgres in production | SQL, GraphQL |
| **Nuthatch** | no | no: tables come from the ABI | your RPC endpoint | one binary | SQL, HTTP, MCP |

Like Ponder, Nuthatch reads the chain over JSON-RPC, so it needs an endpoint, and a provider may
charge for one. The public endpoints it bundles are for trying it out, not for keeping it running.
It complements The Graph rather than replacing it: a subgraph serves an application from a network
of indexers, while a nest puts a contract's history in a database on your own machine.

## Worked example (/example)

The page at https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/example indexes USDC on Ethereum mainnet from its
contract address: `init` vendors the ABI and scaffolds the nest, `nuthatch dev --backfill 300` backfills
the last 300 blocks and follows the tip (plain `nuthatch dev` backfills from the deployment block,
which for USDC wants your own archive-capable RPC), every declared event becomes a table (`usdc__transfer`) with
provenance columns, queryable through read-only SQL over HTTP and MCP, and the page then chooses
between an authored view and a maintained entity. It is the current, executable path on v4.0.2.
Scaffolding from a **subgraph manifest** also ships:
`init --from-subgraph <CID|url>` maps `dataSources` -> `[[contracts]]` and `templates` ->
`[[templates]]`, vendors every ABI from the CID the manifest pins, and carries `startBlock` and each
dataSource's `eventHandlers` across. Factory rules are inferred only where a parameter unambiguously
names a template; anything ambiguous is reported with candidates rather than guessed, because which
template a factory creates lives in the mapping WASM rather than in the manifest.

## Who runs it (/stories)

The page at https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/stories answers "is this for me?" through three
illustrative personas - not testimonials, first names only - each traced end to end through one of
the three front doors: an SQL endpoint (`GET /sql`) for application backends, published nests for
analysts who write no indexing code, and the built-in MCP server for agents. These workflows run on
v4.0.2: multi-contract nests, every declared event as a table, nine built-in chains, user-authored
views, maintained `entities.toml` relations, `init --from`, `/sql`, and MCP all ship, as do
factories, the compliance pack, the admin UI, and webhooks. GraphQL is not one of the front doors:
the read surface shipped in 3.7.0 is partial and parked. The page also names one real production user - Lodestar, a public Graph Protocol dashboard,
serving two panels live from a single nuthatch binary. The page states the freshness caveat plainly - derived views read
finalized data, raw event tables are fresh to the tip. Do not infer customers, quotes, or benchmark
numbers from it.

## Roadmap (/roadmap)

The page at https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/roadmap is generated from the source repo, not from
memory. The README's working-now table and progress log are the source of truth for what is
shipped; the numbered RFCs under `docs/rfcs/` are the source of truth for what is planned; where
the README and the page disagree, the README wins. Reading key: shipped = merged with tests and,
where relevant, a measured number; in progress = partially landed, remainder tracked; planned = an
RFC written in the repo, not yet started; not planned = a deliberate scope decision. Dates are not
promised - order is.

- Shipped: the embedded single-binary pipeline end to end (multi-contract ABI-driven decode of
  every declared event, provenance/ergonomics columns - `block_hash`, `_seq`, `block_timestamp`,
  `*_dec`/`*_overflow` - reorg-safe hot store, finality-sealed content-addressed Parquet, DuckDB
  SQL over `/tables` + `/table/{name}` and `/sql` (hot tip UNION sealed history), an i128 DBSP balance
  view with restart-replay, HTTP + a 12-tool/3-resource/3-prompt offline MCP server); nests
  (`init --from`, vendored ABIs + deploy blocks, schema versioning, authored drift-gated `views/*.sql`
  (RFC-0018), the `nuthatch check` parity framework);
  nine built-in chains (Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, Base, BSC, Polygon, Gnosis, Optimism, Monad,
  Robinhood Chain) with finality as policy, and any other EVM chain via `--rpc`; the complete
  backfill work (RFC-0004: bench harness, seal-direct, pipelined fetching, adaptive chunker,
  `dev --seal-direct`) with byte-identical segments across paths and no throughput multiplier claimed
  until the corrected harness has a deterministic replay source; factory/dynamic contract discovery
  (RFC-0009 - it indexes Uniswap); the
  compliance pack (RFC-0008 complete - screening, threshold/velocity flags, counterparty exposure,
  alert webhooks, signed pack manifest + reproducible `audit replay`); a local admin UI + webhooks
  with HMAC-signed egress (RFC-0010); content-addressed nest packaging (RFC-0012 - `nest bundle`/
  `load`, a portable `.bundle` loadable from a file or a URL); the operator surface (Prometheus `/metrics`, `/sql` guards - timeout, row cap,
  result-byte ceiling, concurrency, a filesystem denylist, single-statement enforcement - graceful
  shutdown, a published stability contract); pure zero-capability WASM
  transforms plus effectful `kv`-capability stages; the delightful core (RFC-0015: sql/REPL, magical
  init, add, prod recipes) and the governed semantic layer + agent-grade MCP (RFC-0016/0017); the
  nest registry (RFC-0019); N-1 upgrades (RFC-0020); multichain runtimes
  (RFC-0021); derive-first recipes and pinned `eth_call` (RFC-0023 tiers 1-3); adaptive MCP tools
  (RFC-0025); fault quarantine and partial health (RFC-0026); live mount and unmount with no
  co-tenant restart (RFC-0027); `eth_getLogs` range-control hardening (RFC-0028); the tenant runtime
  that retired the roost and keyed nest data by content address (RFC-0032); identity and grafting
  (RFC-0033); the query allowlist (RFC-0034); verified IPFS resolution (RFC-0037); subgraph-manifest
  scaffolding (RFC-0038); distributed scaled mode (RFC-0022); sealed segments mirrored to a bucket
  (RFC-0052) and DuneSQL queries emitted for a nest (RFC-0055); proven, typed IPFS documents at
  scale (RFC-0037 slices 5 to 8); offchain price snapshots (RFC-0045 stage 2); the 3.11.0 RPC
  economies; v4.0.2 the current release with prebuilt binaries and container images;
  a CI RAM-budget gate with a measured footprint (~37 MB single contract, ~58 MB
  three-contract 23-table nest, 2.8% of 2 GB).
- **The 2026 feature freeze is over.** It ran from 2026-08-20 to 2026-09-08 and was lifted in full.
  The work since is the RFC-0044 to RFC-0048 programme (the subgraph port, offchain data, x402 at the
  counter, the lakehouse commitments, pricing query access), plus RFC-0053, RFC-0052 and RFC-0055.
- In progress: replacing DuckDB with Burrmill (in shadow on main, in no release yet).
- Accepted and then parked on 2026-09-26: RFC-0058 (cross-nest SQL), RFC-0059 (checkpointed folds,
  built in part behind the off-by-default `folds` feature) and RFC-0060 (the Network Subgraph
  endpoint).
- Deferred, not cancelled, and reopened one item at a time (`docs/frozen-for-2027.md` in the
  nuthatch repo): the Lodestar migration (RFC-0011 - pilot live in production, two panels
  serving from one nuthatch binary; remaining panels outstanding); reth ExEx wiring (RFC-0003 -
  Source trait, library split, and bridge in and tested; needs a synced node); the remaining release
  engineering (RFC-0005 - signed artifacts, a Homebrew tap); firehose-class extraction of traces and
  state diffs (RFC-0014, gated on ExEx); IVM generalisation;
  effectful HTTP egress for transform worlds; wildcard indexing.
- Not planned: a token or decentralized-network features, telemetry of any kind, a Kubernetes-first
  deployment, and any gateway/auth/metering layer in the core.

## Install

v4.0.2 is the current release. The installer and `cargo` fetch the latest.

**4.0.2 narrows a result cap sent under the rate-limit code.** An `eth_getLogs` refused with `-32005` and
"query returned more than 10000 results", as `rpc.mevblocker.io` answers, is narrowed to the suggested
range instead of being retried at the same width.

**4.0.1 changes the mainnet defaults.** A new Ethereum mainnet nest gets `mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co` and
`rpc.mevblocker.io`, replacing two public endpoints that could not serve a backfill. An existing nest
keeps the endpoints in its `nuthatch.toml`; `--rpc` overrides them at runtime.

**4.0.0 is the stable line.** It is 3.13.3 plus three small fixes, and the major version is a promise
about later releases rather than a claim about what changed. Upgrading from 3.13.3 is a binary swap:
no storage migration, config change, NID change or re-index. A backfill whose RPC endpoints cannot
serve its history says so: an endpoint that has pruned the range is named with the remedy (an
archive-capable RPC via `--rpc` or `rpc_urls`), a backfill stops on the first refusal when every
endpoint has pruned it, one that makes no progress stops with its cause, and a runtime hosting mounts
warns with the same text and keeps retrying. `nuthatch sql` and the MCP SQL tool print columns in the
query's order, not alphabetically, and a `/sql` response gains a `columns` array naming them in that
order; row objects are unchanged, and `nuthatch sql --json` still prints them with sorted keys. The
first-run demo starts near the tip with `nuthatch dev --backfill 300` (the last 300 blocks, about an
hour of mainnet); when a from-deployment backfill is long, `init` prints a `nuthatch dev --backfill N`
line under its `next:` hint and `dev` logs the span at cold start. Plain `nuthatch dev` still
backfills from the contract's deployment block, which for USDC is 20 million blocks and wants your own
archive-capable RPC.

**The 4.x promise.** From 4.0.0 to the last 4.x release: config keeps working with the same meaning;
a data directory written by an earlier 4.x opens in place on a later one, with no re-index, re-seal or
migration command; and no HTTP route, response field, generated table or column, or MCP tool is
removed, renamed or retyped. It is upgrade only. A released 4.x only gets patches, features wait for
the monthly minor (4.1, 4.2), and correctness and security fixes ship immediately. Not covered:
downgrades; the off-by-default cargo features `graph`, `folds`, `counter`, `exex` and
`shadow-burrmill`; the SQL dialect's functions, which are DuckDB's; segment hashes across `arrow-rs`
versions; the admin UI's HTML; and the `postgres-store` build's internal schema. The full contract is
`docs/operators.md#stability-contract` in the nuthatch repository.

**3.9.0 to 3.13.3.** 3.9.0 adds `nest nid` and `offchain pull`, and offchain snapshots reach authored
entities. Two configurations 3.8.5 accepted now refuse to start: an entity whose `sql` is inline or
names a file other than `entities/<name>.sql`, and a contract alias or template name that would put
its tables inside `offchain__`. An `eth_call` item error is no longer stored as a revert: only an
explicit revert is, and anything else is retried and then stalls the nest at that block, so a nest
calling through a pruned endpoint needs an archive one. 3.10.0 moves the GraphQL routes behind
`--features graph` (the published binary answers them with 404; `init --from-subgraph`, `port-emit`
and `graph-validate` stay in the default build) and lets a second live mount share an already-mounted
dataset. 3.11.0 cuts the RPC bill: timestamps from the logs (4,444 header reads down to 34 on the same
20,000-block Sepolia backfill, byte-identical segments), the chain's block time as the default poll
interval, and `--rpc-fallback`. 3.12.0 changes nothing in the published binaries; its work is behind
the off-by-default `folds` feature. 3.12.1 executes each `/sql` statement once rather than twice, and
answers a query cut off by the time budget with 504 rather than 400. 3.12.2 moves Wasmtime past two security advisories, holds a nest mounted on a running runtime to the rules boot enforces, lets a runtime start with nothing mounted, and reads a provider's wrapped revert and block-range cap correctly. 3.13.0 lets a runtime run its own nests: handed a NID, it fetches the nest from a registry, verifies and indexes it as a job readable over the admin API, and can dry-run, suspend, resume, move and reclaim it; `/metrics` reports storage per nest, and the runtime-wide sealed total no longer counts a shared store once per nest. 3.13.1 fixes what an end-to-end run of that admin API found against a real chain: names and a restart mid-move that left a runtime unable to start, a move that broke a dataset two tenants shared, and identical mounts reported as failed; routes are now keyed per mount, so a mount of a single non-default tenant serves at `/<tenant>/<alias>/`, and `/metrics` is served at the runtime root. 3.13.3 makes `nuthatch check` lower and bind each entity as `dev` starts it, so the two agree; makes every entity `port-emit` writes startable; makes `nest bundle` refuse to publish credentials; stops log lines keeping an RPC URL's password; and makes a restart, an idle entity fault and a finality violation report truthfully. 3.13.2 fixes what a hardening pass found: Arbitrum timestamps stored as 0 through `arb1.arbitrum.io` (now fetched as headers, in batches of ten that `arb1` takes, so a backfill through keyless `arb1` runs at a few times chain speed), an analytics spill cap DuckDB did not enforce (now enforced, 2 GB by default, off a tmpfs `/tmp`), authored entity columns reaching SQL as text, and misspelt `nuthatch.toml` keys silently ignored (now a warning, a `check` failure, and a suggestion). Each is a binary swap and a
restart, apart from the 3.9.0 refusals and the 3.10.0 GraphQL routes, and from 3.13.0 a script that mounts over the admin API adds `?wait=true`.

**3.8.0 makes an `[[ipfs]]` nest over megabyte documents fit to deploy.** It was built for Edge &
Node's QoS oracle on Gnosis. Every document a nest names resolves behind the cursor, is proven against
its CID however many blocks it spans, and can be exploded into typed rows (`[ipfs.rows]`), and a seal
cut is also bounded at 64 MiB of row JSON, so sealing those documents stays inside the memory budget.
It adds `--cors <ORIGIN>` on `dev` and `serve` (it grants reach, not access; every guard still
applies), `--explorer <URL>` on `init` and `add` for a Blockscout instance, `init --from-subgraph` over
a local `subgraph.yaml`, and a `doctor` that finds its own probe address without `--address`. `/sql`
and `/explain` answer `503` when the hot tip holds more than 64 MiB of row JSON, and a `/sql` request
waits up to 250 ms for a free permit before it is told the node is busy. No CLI flag, config key or
metric was removed or renamed. An events-only nest keeps its identity and data and swaps the binary.
A nest with `[[calls]]` or `[[ipfs]]` adopts its full decode identity on first start without a
re-index, but a nest that has indexed top-level calls must re-index, because call rows now carry the
sender as `tx_from`; a nest with `[extract] traces` also gets a new identity. An `[[ipfs]]` name or
`[ipfs.rows]` table declared twice or landing on an event or call table, and a decoded call argument
named `tx_from`, now refuse to start. Downgrading to 3.7.0 is safe for an events-only nest and refused
for any other after one start on 3.8.

**3.8.1 to 3.8.5 are binary-swap patches, with no identity, configuration or segment change.** 3.8.1
checks an empty document body against its CID rather than retrying immutable bytes ten times. 3.8.2
logs and counts every retried document fetch (`nuthatch_nest_ipfs_retries_total`), grows the fetch
timeout from 30 to 60 to 120 s, bounds a `--seal-direct` window's wait for one document with
`--ipfs-window-deadline` (300 s by default), lists documents given up on at `GET /ipfs/gave-up`, adds
`seal_direct_concurrency`, `seal_direct_ipfs_window_deadline_secs` and `ipfs_gave_up_documents` to
`/ready`, and holds a hot-mounted nest to one backfill window at a time on a single-endpoint chain.
3.8.3 keys a runtime nest's cursor, health and metrics by the route it is served under, so where the
route differs from the nest's name the `nest` label on `nuthatch_nest_*` series is the route and
unmounting the route stops its cursor; `emit dune` translates authored views whose DuneSQL is exact.
3.8.4 refuses to start a store whose data no longer matches what `nuthatch.toml` covers
(`indexed_coverage`); the first start after upgrading records rather than verifies, and a downgrade to
3.8.3 is safe. 3.8.5 fixes a `/sql` panic when DuckDB returned a scaled `DECIMAL` too wide for the
driver, now re-executed as exact strings, and sealed velocity seeds that were skipped silently because
a window start used `/` where it needed integer division.

**3.7.0 mirrors sealed segments to a bucket and emits DuneSQL.** `nuthatch publish sync|verify|status`
and `--publish-target` on `dev`/`serve` (RFC-0052); `nuthatch emit dune` (RFC-0055). The DuckDB memory
walls are environment settings with unchanged defaults and refuse a query rather than shrink, new
seals are zstd with the writer profile named in the catalogue, a declared query (`/q/{name}`) answers
`422` when its plan could read more than 512 MiB or could rescan, and a local offchain file drop
stores a file as an immutable snapshot outside the chain seal. The x402 counter and `nuthatch settle`
exist only in a `--features counter` build; no release binary contains them. A nest with a ported
`graph/schema.graphql` answers GraphQL as a partial read surface, exact or refused by name field by
field, that is parked and is not a drop-in replacement for a subgraph. Most operators swap the binary
and restart. The exceptions: `NUTHATCH_SQL_MAX_CONCURRENCY` above 2 refuses to start unless
`NUTHATCH_ANALYTICS_MEMORY_LIMIT` comes down (256MB at four permits), and a nest with a fully named,
non-indexed tuple event parameter gets a new NID and re-indexes (#1364). Downgrading to 3.6.1 after
running 3.7.0 is not safe.

**3.0.0 makes authored incremental entities stable.** An entity declared in `entities.toml` is a
bounded keyed relation maintained while blocks arrive, not a view recomputed at query time. Existing
nests upgrade by binary swap with no migration or re-index; adding an entity seeds it from local stored
history at the next restart. `--seal-direct` refuses an entity-bearing nest. Release artifacts carry
GitHub build-provenance attestations, verifiable with `gh attestation verify <tarball> --repo
nightswatchhq/nuthatch`.

**2.7.0 made `[[calls]]` and `--seal-direct` compatible.** Every direct-seal path resolves the
pinned reads before committing. Factory backfills narrow on a provider cap in the newly-discovered
child pass; declared-but-unfired events resolve as empty typed tables; a stale `schema.json` no longer
hides live registry columns; `doctor --dir` probes the full contract set; timestamp retry splits run
concurrently; and benchmark output redacts state-RPC credentials. It is a binary swap with no config
change, migration or re-index.

- Prebuilt binaries for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Linux x86_64 on the GitHub release, with SHA-256
  checksums; the one-line installer (`curl -fsSL https://nuthatch-indexer.com/install.sh | sh`)
  downloads and verifies them. Read any install script before running it.
- `cargo +1.95.0 install --git https://github.com/nightswatchhq/nuthatch nuthatch` (**exactly 1.95.0** - `rust-toolchain.toml` does not apply to `cargo install`, and 1.97 hits a dbsp ICE).
- Container images are published per release at `ghcr.io/nightswatchhq/nuthatch` (`:<version>` and
  `:<version>-scaled`). A Homebrew tap and detached release signatures (minisign/cosign) are on the
  way; embedded mode needs no Docker.

## Scope

In scope: EVM chains, embedded mode (built) and scaled mode (built, opt-in at build time), the workflow above. Out
of scope: any gateway, auth, metering, or multi-tenancy layer in the core (those are an operator's
layer, not the binary's); any token, staking, or decentralized-network feature; telemetry of any
kind; non-EVM chains before EVM is airtight; trusted-execution attestation or zero-knowledge proofs.
